rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
m1 c1 / t1 = m2 c2 / t2 when K and the interval match
c2 = m1 c1 t2 / (m2 t1)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: A longer time means a larger heat capacity, not automatically a larger specific heat, because mass also matters.  ·  Neglect W only when the question allows it.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Record the room temperature so you can show the excess was modest.  ·  A dirty or wet outer surface changes K.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: An unknown specific heat can be found by timing how long the liquid takes to cool through a chosen interval, then repeating the run with water in the same calorimeter.  ·  Newton's law says the time is proportional to the heat capacity when the surface factor and the temperature limits are unchanged. So (m_u c_u + W) / t_u = (m_w c_w + W) / t_w if the water equivalent W of the cup is included.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The two runs must share the upper and lower temperatures.  ·  Cooling gives c. It is not a latent-heat measurement.

rows.label: Derivation

rows.text: Equal masses of water and an unknown liquid cool through the same interval in 6.0 min and 4.0 min. Neglect the cup. Find c_u if c_w = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: If the question says the calorimeter has negligible heat capacity, this collapses to m_u c_u / t_u = m_w c_w / t_w.  ·  Water is the known standard, with c_w about 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1. The unknown c is then c_u = c_w (m_w / m_u) (t_u / t_w).  ·  The interval must be the same pair of temperatures, for example 80°C down to 70°C, and the room must not have changed between the runs.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Write whether W was included.  ·  Convert minutes to seconds only if you also want a value of K. The ratio of times does not need that.  ·  c_u = c_w (m_w t_u) / (m_u t_w) if W = 0.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Write m1 c1 / t1 = m2 c2 / t2 when K and the interval match and say what each symbol means.  ·  Mark the known values, then substitute one step at a time.  ·  Finish with the number, the unit, and the direction when the quantity has one.
